Synthesis faithfully used the retrieved evidence, so changing the wording prompt would miss the cause.
The team fixes freshness ranking and adds the case to retrieval regression tests.
caseStudy.result: The correct subsystem is repaired without destabilizing parts that already work.
caseStudy.danger: One blended quality score can improve while a small but high-risk slice becomes dangerously worse.
caseStudy.takeaway: Pair an end-to-end outcome with stage metrics, slices, and evidence that identifies the source of failure.

lessons.lab: For one failed answer, define one metric at each of the six stages and show which evidence would prove where the problem began.
lessons.checkpoint: Why is end-to-end accuracy alone insufficient for debugging?
lessons.answer: It reports the final outcome but does not identify which stage caused it.

lessons.title: Latency and cost budgets
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create a horizontal 10 SECOND REQUEST BUDGET split into ROUTING 0.3S, RETRIEVAL 1.2S, MODEL 2.5S, TOOLS 3.0S, SPECIALIST 2.0S, UI 1.0S. Below it show a COST BUDGET with MODEL TOKENS, SEARCH, TOOL CALLS, STORAGE. Add coral budget alerts, a teal FAST PATH, a blue DEEP PATH, and a small decision gate labeled VALUE JUSTIFIES COST?
lessons.alt: A ten-second request budget and a separate cost budget allocate limits to routing, retrieval, models, tools, specialist work, and the interface, with fast and deep paths chosen by expected value.
lessons.outcome: Treat time and money as design inputs instead of surprises found after launch.
lessons.explanation: A production request has a user-visible latency target and a cost ceiling. Allocate both across stages, reserve time for the interface and recovery, and stop work that can no longer finish usefully. Percentiles reveal slow-tail pain better than averages. Choose a fast path for simple cases and a deeper path only when complexity, risk, or value justifies it.
trace: The product sets an end-to-end target based on what the user can tolerate.
Architects allocate stage budgets and concurrency without double-counting parallel work.
Runtime deadlines and token or tool limits flow into downstream calls.
Telemetry records actual latency and cost by stage, percentile, and request class.
Routing chooses fast, deep, deferred, or human paths before the budget is exhausted.
lessons.analogy: A holiday budget assigns money to travel, hotel, food, and emergencies. Spending everything on the first item leaves no way to finish the trip.
nextjs: Next.js records server timing and streams meaningful progress before the full result is ready.
Route policy selects a fast answer, deep workflow, or deferred task from request risk and complexity.
Usage and cost summaries remain server-side while the UI receives safe progress and final outcomes.
python: Python clients accept deadlines, retry limits, and usage budgets through typed request context.
Concurrent independent work is joined with explicit remaining-time checks and cancellation.
Metrics report p50, p95, and p99 latency plus model, retrieval, tool, and infrastructure cost.

caseStudy.situation: Acme's agent produces excellent refund summaries, but difficult cases sometimes take forty seconds and cost ten times more than normal.
walkthrough: Tracing shows three serial searches and two specialist calls occur even for simple status questions.
A fast path answers verified status requests with one retrieval and one narrow tool.
Complex disputes become durable tasks with visible progress instead of holding one request open.
Dashboards compare latency and cost by path, outcome, and percentile.
caseStudy.result: Simple cases become fast and predictable while expensive work is used only where it adds value.
caseStudy.danger: Optimizing only the average hides the slow tail, and cutting cost blindly can remove the evidence or safeguards that create quality.
caseStudy.takeaway: Allocate explicit latency and cost budgets, measure the tail, and spend more only when the user value requires it.

lessons.lab: Create a ten-second and one-dollar budget for a six-stage request. Define the fallback when any stage reaches 80 percent of its allocation.
lessons.checkpoint: Why should a user-interface budget exist inside the end-to-end latency target?
lessons.answer: The user experiences rendering and communication too; a fast backend can still feel slow if the interface has no time or progress design.

lessons.title: Red-team and incident learning loop
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create a circular reliability loop labeled THREAT MODEL, ATTACK TESTS, DETECT, CONTAIN, INVESTIGATE, FIX, REGRESSION TEST, RELEASE SAFELY. Feed REAL INCIDENT and NEAR MISS cards into INVESTIGATE. Show coral attack paths for INJECTION, EXCESSIVE ACTION, DATA LEAK, CROSS-TENANT, RETRY DUPLICATE and teal verified controls returning to RELEASE SAFELY.
lessons.alt: Threat modeling, attack tests, detection, containment, investigation, fixes, and regression tests form a learning loop fed by incidents and near misses before a safer release.
lessons.outcome: Make every serious failure improve both the system and the tests that guard it.
lessons.explanation: Red teaming deliberately explores how the system can fail; incident response handles failures that occur. Both should produce concrete controls and repeatable regression cases. The team preserves evidence, contains impact, identifies technical and process causes, fixes the smallest trustworthy boundary, verifies it against attack and normal cases, and records ownership and follow-up.
trace: Threat modeling identifies assets, boundaries, attackers, misuse, and unacceptable outcomes.
Attack tests exercise hostile content, permissions, tenants, retries, cancellations, and data paths.
Detection rules and runbooks turn signals into timely containment.
Investigation reconstructs the trace, decisions, policy, data, and blast radius.
The fix ships only after a regression test proves the failure cannot silently return.
lessons.analogy: A fire drill teaches people where alarms, doors, and meeting points fail before a real fire. After a real event, the building plan is updated too.
nextjs: Administrative routes expose privacy-safe incident references, ownership, severity, and remediation state.
Feature flags or kill switches disable one dangerous capability without taking the whole application offline.
The interface gives affected users clear status and recovery steps without exposing security details.
python: Attack tests run as fixtures against policy gates, tool adapters, tenant stores, and recovery logic.
Incident tooling queries traces and immutable receipts while preserving access control and chain of evidence.
Regression suites combine the exploit case with nearby normal cases to prevent an over-broad fix.

caseStudy.situation: A near miss shows that a repeated payment callback could create two refund adjustments during a network failure.
walkthrough: Acme disables automatic payment adjustment above the safe threshold and preserves the affected trace.
Investigation finds that the adapter created a new idempotency key on every retry.
The key is bound to the stable business operation, and duplicate callbacks return the original receipt.
A permanent test simulates lost responses, retries, restarts, and concurrent duplicates before release.
caseStudy.result: The duplicate path is contained, corrected, and converted into evidence that guards future versions.
caseStudy.danger: A post-incident document without a regression test or owner may describe the lesson while allowing the same code path to return.
caseStudy.takeaway: Close the loop: detect, contain, learn, test, assign, verify, and release with evidence.

lessons.lab: Choose one agent-system failure. Write the threat, detection signal, containment action, evidence to preserve, root cause, fix, owner, and regression test.
lessons.checkpoint: When is an incident truly closed?
lessons.answer: After impact is contained, causes and scope are understood, fixes are verified, regression tests and owners exist, and required follow-up is tracked.

lessons.title: MCP, A2A, and AG-UI together
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create three connected ownership lanes. Top lane AG-UI labeled USER EXPERIENCE with USER, REACT APP, EVENTS, SHARED STATE, INTERRUPTS. Middle lane A2A labeled AGENT COLLABORATION with ORCHESTRATOR AGENT, SPECIALIST AGENT, TASK, ARTIFACT. Bottom lane MCP labeled TOOLS AND CONTEXT with MCP CLIENT, MCP SERVER, TOOL, RESOURCE. Use cyan arrows downward for requests and teal arrows upward for results. Add three white cards: USER SEES PROGRESS, AGENTS SHARE WORK, TOOLS DO BOUNDED ACTIONS.
lessons.alt: Three stacked lanes give AG-UI responsibility for the live user experience, A2A responsibility for agent collaboration and task artifacts, and MCP responsibility for bounded tools and context.
lessons.outcome: Give each protocol one clear job and connect them without mixing their responsibilities.
lessons.explanation: These protocols solve different boundaries. MCP standardizes how an application or agent reaches tools and context. A2A standardizes how independent agents advertise abilities and exchange tasks, messages, status, and artifacts. AG-UI carries typed agent-to-user events, shared state, progress, and human interaction. A product may use all three, but it should not force every internal function through a network protocol.
trace: The React application sends user intent and receives a typed AG-UI event stream.
The orchestrator decides whether local work, an MCP capability, or an A2A specialist is needed.
MCP calls return bounded tool results or context to the requesting agent.
A2A work progresses as a task and returns messages or artifacts.
AG-UI translates internal progress and outcomes into a coherent user experience.
lessons.analogy: Think of a hospital: the patient conversation is the user interface, departments coordinate referrals, and instruments perform narrow clinical actions.
nextjs: React renders typed AG-UI events for messages, progress, tools, artifacts, state changes, and approval requests.
Next.js server code owns user identity, policy, orchestration, and adapters to MCP and A2A boundaries.
Internal functions remain ordinary typed modules when interoperability is unnecessary.
python: FastAPI exposes agent endpoints and translates domain events into the AG-UI stream.
A2A client and server adapters map external tasks to internal workflow IDs and artifacts.
MCP adapters expose narrowly typed capabilities and keep authorization in the server boundary.

caseStudy.situation: Maya asks Acme to investigate a disputed refund and prepare an adjustment for approval.
walkthrough: AG-UI shows Maya's request, current progress, evidence cards, and any approval interruption.
The orchestrator delegates payment verification to an A2A specialist task.
The specialist uses an MCP banking tool with limited scope and returns a verified artifact.
The orchestrator combines that artifact with policy evidence and streams the result back through AG-UI.
caseStudy.result: Maya experiences one understandable workflow while each technical boundary stays replaceable and auditable.
caseStudy.danger: Calling every tool an agent or using one protocol for every boundary creates unnecessary coupling and hides ownership.
caseStudy.takeaway: Use MCP for capabilities, A2A for independent agent work, and AG-UI for the live human experience.

lessons.lab: Take one feature and draw its user events, agent tasks, tool calls, state owners, and trust boundaries. Remove any protocol boundary that adds no interoperability value.
lessons.checkpoint: Which protocol carries live progress and human interaction to the React interface?
lessons.answer: AG-UI; A2A handles agent collaboration and MCP handles tools and context.

lessons.title: The typed agent event stream
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create a left-to-right event timeline labeled RUN STARTED, STEP STARTED, TEXT DELTA, TOOL CALL STARTED, TOOL CALL RESULT, STATE SNAPSHOT, ARTIFACT READY, RUN FINISHED. Under it show a REACT REDUCER turning events into CHAT, PROGRESS, TOOL CARD, STATE PANEL, ARTIFACT CARD. Add EVENT ID and RUN ID tags and a coral RECONNECT arrow resuming AFTER LAST EVENT.
lessons.alt: A typed event timeline with run and event IDs drives React views for chat, progress, tools, shared state, and artifacts, while reconnection resumes after the last applied event.
lessons.outcome: Build the interface from explicit events rather than parsing human-readable text for hidden state.
lessons.explanation: A typed event stream is an ordered record of what changed during a run. The client reducer applies each known event to visible state. Stable run and event IDs support deduplication, reconnection, and replay; snapshots repair drift when necessary. Text remains content, while progress, tool activity, artifacts, errors, and approvals remain structured data.
trace: RUN STARTED creates one visible run with a stable identity.
Step, text, and tool events update their own interface regions without guessing from prose.
STATE SNAPSHOT establishes an authoritative recoverable view of shared state.
ARTIFACT READY adds a durable output that can be opened independently.
On reconnect, the client requests events after its last applied event ID.
lessons.analogy: A railway information board consumes timetable events. It does not read a station announcement and guess which row to update.
nextjs: A TypeScript discriminated union defines every supported event and payload.
A pure reducer applies idempotent events and separates durable state from temporary animation state.
The transport reconnects with the last event ID and rejects unknown or invalid payloads safely.
python: Pydantic models validate event envelopes and typed payloads before streaming them.
The server stores or regenerates the replay window associated with a run.
Workflow and protocol adapters emit domain events without embedding interface-specific markup.

caseStudy.situation: Maya's browser loses Wi-Fi after the payment specialist finishes but before the final answer appears.
walkthrough: Her client remembers the last applied event ID and reconnects to the same run.
The server replays the missing artifact and completion events.
The reducer ignores the duplicate tool result that Maya had already applied.
The interface reaches the same state as an uninterrupted run.
caseStudy.result: Maya continues without restarting the business operation or seeing duplicated cards.
caseStudy.danger: If progress and tool state are encoded inside ordinary text, the client cannot validate, resume, deduplicate, or render them reliably.
caseStudy.takeaway: Use typed, ordered, replayable events with stable identities and an idempotent client reducer.

lessons.lab: Define eight event types for one run. For each, write its payload, reducer effect, replay behavior, and what happens if it arrives twice.
lessons.checkpoint: Why must the client reducer be idempotent?
lessons.answer: Reconnects and delivery retries can repeat events, so applying the same event twice must not duplicate effects.

lessons.title: Progress, artifacts, and recovery UX
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create a three-column agent interface blueprint. Column one LIVE PROGRESS has steps UNDERSTANDING, CHECKING POLICY, VERIFYING PAYMENT, PREPARING RESULT. Column two ARTIFACTS has EVIDENCE PACK, DECISION SUMMARY, AUDIT RECEIPT. Column three RECOVERY has RETRY SAFE STEP, CONTINUE TASK, CHANGE INPUT, CONTACT HUMAN. Add a coral PARTIAL FAILURE between progress and recovery, plus a teal COMPLETED EARLIER badge on preserved artifacts.
lessons.alt: A user interface separates live progress, durable artifacts, and recovery choices so a partial failure preserves completed work and offers a safe next step.
lessons.outcome: Show users useful state without exposing private reasoning or pretending uncertain work is finished.
lessons.explanation: Good agentic UX answers four questions: what is happening, what has completed, what is available now, and what can the user do next? Progress should describe observable stages, not hidden reasoning. Artifacts have names, versions, sources, and status. Errors explain impact and recovery in plain language. Completed durable work remains available when a later stage fails.
trace: The interface names the current business stage and completed stages.
Artifacts appear as addressable cards as soon as they are valid and safe to expose.
A partial failure identifies which step failed and which work remains preserved.
Recovery choices distinguish safe retry, resume, edit input, cancel, and human help.
The final state summarizes result, evidence, remaining uncertainty, and trace reference.
lessons.analogy: A delivery app shows preparing, collected, and arriving, then preserves the order details if the driver has a problem. It does not reveal the dispatcher's private conversation.
nextjs: React derives stage cards and recovery controls from typed events and server-provided permitted actions.
Artifact routes use stable IDs, authorization checks, versions, and accessible download or preview states.
Error components state impact, preserved work, and the next safe choice without exposing stack traces.
python: FastAPI status models return public stage, progress, artifact references, recovery actions, and support-safe error codes.
Workflow checkpoints mark which outputs are durable and which step can be retried or resumed.
Artifact storage and audit records keep ownership, provenance, hashes, and lifecycle state.

caseStudy.situation: Maya's refund investigation finishes its evidence pack, but the payment specialist times out while preparing the adjustment.
walkthrough: The progress panel marks policy and evidence complete and payment preparation interrupted.
The verified evidence pack remains available with its version and sources.
Maya can resume the same task, change the proposed amount, cancel, or request a human review.
A resumed run reuses completed evidence and starts only the safe unfinished step.
caseStudy.result: Maya understands the interruption, keeps useful work, and can recover without duplicating the refund.
caseStudy.danger: A spinner followed by a generic error makes users repeat work and cannot explain whether any side effect already happened.
caseStudy.takeaway: Design progress around observable stages, artifacts around durable value, and recovery around safe permitted choices.

lessons.lab: Draw the progress, artifact, error, and recovery states for a three-step workflow where step two succeeds and step three times out after an unknown response.
lessons.checkpoint: Should the interface display the model's hidden chain of thought as progress?
lessons.answer: No. Show concise observable stages, evidence, actions, and outcomes rather than private internal reasoning.

lessons.title: Interrupts, approval, and human steering
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create an active run flowing from PLAN to CHECK POLICY to PAUSE. At PAUSE show a large APPROVAL CARD with PROPOSED ACTION, EVIDENCE, RISK, EXPIRES, APPROVE, REJECT, EDIT. Add separate steering controls ADD CONTEXT, CHANGE PRIORITY, CANCEL. Then show REVALIDATE leading to RESUME or coral INVALIDATE AND REPLAN. Include a white card labeled NEW INPUT NEVER SILENTLY REWRITES COMPLETED ACTIONS.
lessons.alt: An active run pauses on an approval card, accepts explicit approval or steering, revalidates changed state, and either resumes or creates a new plan without silently rewriting completed actions.
lessons.outcome: Keep people in control while preserving the integrity of the workflow and audit trail.
lessons.explanation: An interrupt is a deliberate pause that requests missing input, permission, or a decision. Approval concerns one exact proposed action; steering changes goals, constraints, or priorities. Both are authenticated events recorded against a workflow version. New input may invalidate the old plan, so the system rechecks policy, evidence, deadlines, and already completed side effects before resuming.
trace: The workflow reaches a state that cannot safely continue without a human decision.
The interface presents the exact proposal, evidence, risk, alternatives, and expiry.
The person's approval, rejection, edit, context, priority change, or cancellation becomes a typed event.
The server revalidates current state and determines whether the old plan is still safe.
The run resumes, replans, compensates, or ends with a complete audit history.
lessons.analogy: Changing a flight after one leg has already been flown requires a new route from the current airport, not pretending the journey restarted at home.
nextjs: React renders distinct controls for approve, reject, edit, add context, reprioritize, and cancel.
Server actions bind decisions to user identity, proposal ID, workflow version, and anti-replay protection.
The interface disables stale controls and explains when new information requires a new proposal.
python: FastAPI endpoints validate typed interrupt responses and append them to workflow history.
The workflow engine compares expected and current state before moving from paused to running.
Domain logic prevents completed side effects from being silently undone or repeated after steering.

caseStudy.situation: While Maya waits for approval of a $120 refund adjustment, the customer provides evidence that the correct amount is $95.
walkthrough: Maya edits the proposed amount and adds the new evidence through explicit steering controls.
The old $120 proposal and its pending approval are invalidated, not mutated invisibly.
Policy and evidence are rechecked, producing a new $95 proposal with a new identity.
The supervisor approves that exact proposal and execution writes one matching receipt.
caseStudy.result: The final action matches the latest evidence while the history clearly explains every change.
caseStudy.danger: Treating any chat message as approval can authorize the wrong version, and resuming without revalidation can repeat or contradict completed work.
caseStudy.takeaway: Make human input typed and explicit, bind it to exact state, then revalidate before continuing.

lessons.lab: Design one approval interrupt and three steering actions. State what each invalidates, what must be rechecked, and what audit event is written.
lessons.checkpoint: Is editing a proposal the same as approving it?
lessons.answer: No. An edit invalidates the original proposal and requires a newly identified proposal and any required review.

lessons.title: Production capstone: Acme Agent Desk
lessons.diagramPrompt: Create a polished complete architecture map titled only ACME AGENT DESK. Left: USER and NEXT.JS REACT EXPERIENCE with AG-UI EVENTS, AUTH, APPROVALS, ARTIFACTS. Center: ORCHESTRATOR, DURABLE WORKFLOW, POLICY GATE, MEMORY AND RAG, EVALS, OBSERVABILITY. Right: A2A PAYMENT SPECIALIST with TASKS AND ARTIFACTS, plus MCP SERVERS POLICY, CASES, BANKING with narrow TOOLS. Bottom: POSTGRES, VECTOR INDEX, QUEUE, ARTIFACT STORE, SECRET MANAGER, AUDIT STORE. Use cyan request paths, teal results, coral denials and human control. Add PYTHON FASTAPI CORE and VERCEL DEPLOYMENT labels without any other branding.
lessons.alt: The complete Acme Agent Desk joins a Next.js and React experience, AG-UI events, a Python and FastAPI core, durable workflows, policy and RAG, A2A specialist tasks, narrow MCP servers, governed storage, evaluations, and observability.
lessons.outcome: Assemble every Volume 3 idea into one explainable full-stack production system.
lessons.explanation: The capstone is a working reference architecture, not one giant agent. The Next.js application owns the accessible user experience and authenticated server boundary. A Python and FastAPI service owns domain orchestration and durable work. MCP servers expose narrow capabilities; an A2A specialist owns independent payment work; AG-UI events keep the user informed and in control. Policy, identity, tenant isolation, idempotency, evidence, evaluation, and telemetry cross every layer.
trace: Maya starts an authenticated case in the Next.js and React application.
AG-UI events show progress while the FastAPI orchestrator checkpoints durable business state.
RAG finds versioned policy evidence and MCP tools read or update narrowly scoped records.
An A2A payment specialist produces a task artifact; high-risk action pauses for exact human approval.
The final artifact, receipt, trace, evaluation evidence, and recovery state remain addressable and auditable.
lessons.analogy: A well-run airport is many coordinated systems: passenger screens, control towers, specialists, gates, baggage, security, records, and recovery plans. No single worker does everything.
nextjs: Next.js App Router provides authenticated pages, server routes, event streaming, approval actions, and artifact views.
React components reduce typed AG-UI events into accessible progress, evidence, tool, task, approval, and recovery states.
Vercel deployment keeps public web concerns separate from long-running durable work and external service boundaries.
python: FastAPI exposes typed domain endpoints, orchestration, policy checks, MCP and A2A adapters, and telemetry middleware.
Durable workers use checkpoints, stable idempotency keys, queues, deadlines, cancellation, and compensating actions.
Postgres, vector search, artifact storage, secrets, and audit repositories enforce tenant and provenance boundaries.

caseStudy.situation: Acme asks Maya to resolve RF-2048 from first question through evidence, payment verification, approval, adjustment, and customer-ready explanation.
walkthrough: Maya signs in, opens the case, and sees its current durable state rather than a blank conversation.
The orchestrator retrieves current policy, checks freshness, and asks the payment specialist for independent verification.
The specialist uses a narrow banking capability and returns a signed artifact; policy produces an exact adjustment proposal.
A supervisor approves the proposal, execution is idempotent, and Maya receives an evidence pack, receipt, trace reference, and clear final explanation.
caseStudy.result: The project demonstrates a trustworthy end-to-end agent product in both TypeScript and Python, with visible evidence for safety, reliability, cost, and user control.
caseStudy.danger: A polished chat screen can conceal missing durability, overpowered tools, stale evidence, weak tenant boundaries, duplicated actions, and no way to prove quality.
caseStudy.takeaway: Build the system as small owned boundaries, then prove each boundary with contracts, traces, evaluations, recovery tests, and understandable user states.

lessons.lab: Create the capstone in six milestones: contracts and threat model; durable state; RAG and MCP; A2A specialist; AG-UI experience and approvals; evaluation, observability, deployment, and recovery drill.
lessons.checkpoint: What makes this a production agent system rather than an impressive demonstration?
lessons.answer: It preserves durable state, bounds authority, uses current evidence, survives retries and failure, keeps people informed and in control, and proves behavior through telemetry and evaluations.
